title: Restorative Drugs (Vitamins and Minerals)
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Restorative Drugs: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content: Restorative drugs are substances used to rebuild bodily health, correct nutritional deficits, and support normal physiological processes. Vitamins are organic compounds required in tiny amounts that the human body generally cannot synthesize on its own, necessitating dietary intake. Minerals are inorganic elements derived from the earth and water, absorbed by plants and eaten by animals. In clinical nursing practice across Nigeria, these agents act as vital coenzymes and structural components. Patients recovering from chronic illnesses, severe malnutrition, or major surgery frequently require supplementation to restore biochemical balance and accelerate recovery.

headings.title: Classification and Sources of Vitamins
headings.content:
Vitamins divide into two primary groups based on solubility, which dictates how the body absorbs, transports, and stores them.

- **Fat-soluble vitamins**: Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in lipids and require dietary fat for absorption via the lymphatic system. Excess amounts are stored in the liver and adipose tissue, creating a higher risk of toxicity if consumed in excessive quantities.
- **Water-soluble vitamins**: The B-complex group and Vitamin C dissolve in water and pass easily into the bloodstream. Excess amounts are readily excreted in the urine, requiring more frequent replenishment through diet or supplementation.

headings.title: Classification and Sources of Minerals
headings.content:
Minerals are categorized by the amount the human body requires daily. Macrominerals are needed in large quantities, whereas trace minerals are required in minute amounts.

| Category | Examples | Primary Dietary Sources |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Macrominerals | Calcium, Potassium, Sodium, Magnesium | Dairy products, green leafy vegetables, table salt |
| Trace Minerals | Iron, Zinc, Iodine, Copper | Red meat, beans, seafood, iodized salt |

headings.title: Pharmacokinetics and Mechanism of Action
headings.content: Once ingested, vitamins and minerals follow distinct pharmacokinetic pathways. Absorption occurs primarily in the small intestine, influenced by gut acidity, presence of binding proteins, and carrier molecules. For instance, intrinsic factor in the gastric mucosa is mandatory for Vitamin B12 absorption. Once absorbed, they circulate bound to plasma proteins or travel freely in plasma to target tissues. Inside cells, they act as coenzymes, cofactors, or structural elements to drive enzymatic reactions, maintain fluid balance, and support cellular replication. Elimination happens mainly through renal excretion for water-soluble substances and biliary excretion for fat-soluble compounds.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Therapeutic Uses
headings.content: Therapeutic supplementation aims to correct confirmed deficiencies, support periods of high physiological demand, and manage specific disease states. Pregnant and lactating women receive routine iron and folic acid to prevent neural tube defects and maternal anemia. Patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis often require water-soluble vitamin replacements due to dialysis loss. Iron supplements treat iron-deficiency anemia, while calcium and Vitamin D combinations manage osteoporosis. Prophylactic doses are also given in communities with high burdens of malnutrition to boost immune resilience.

headings.title: Nutritional Deficiencies and Associated Syndromes
headings.content: Lack of essential vitamins and minerals leads to distinct clinical deficiency syndromes. Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia and night blindness. Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency results in beriberi, commonly seen in populations reliant on polished white rice, or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in chronic alcoholism. Niacin deficiency manifests as pellagra, characterized by the classic 'three Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Iron deficiency produces microcytic anemia, presenting with pallor, fatigue, and weakness.

headings.title: Adverse Effects and Toxicity of Supplementation
headings.content: While essential, excessive intake of vitamins and minerals can cause toxicity, known as hypervitaminosis or mineral poisoning. Fat-soluble vitamins, particularly Vitamin A and D, pose the highest risk of accumulation and harm. Chronic Vitamin A toxicity leads to liver damage, bone pain, and skin peeling. High doses of iron supplements can cause severe gastrointestinal irritation, corrosion of the mucosal lining, and acute poisoning in young children who ingest tablets mistaking them for sweets. Water-soluble vitamins rarely cause toxicity because excess amounts exit through urine, though massive doses of Vitamin C can cause osmotic diarrhea and kidney stones.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment, Patient Education, and Administration Guidelines
headings.content: Nurses play a crucial role in safe restorative drug therapy through thorough assessment, careful administration, and patient education. Assessment involves reviewing dietary habits, checking laboratory values like hemoglobin and serum electrolytes, and screening for deficiency symptoms. When administering oral iron, nurses should advise patients to take it with citrus juice like orange juice to enhance absorption through acidic medium, while warning that stools may turn dark green or black. Injectable iron requires the Z-track method to prevent skin staining. Patient education must emphasize that supplements complement a balanced diet rather than replace whole foods, and containers must be stored safely out of children's reach.
